summary: Sarah Guo of Conviction, an AI-native venture fund launched ~3 years ago, presents at the AI Engineer World's Fair on the state of startups and AI in 2025. She highlights three capability areas: reasoning as a new scaling vector for intelligence, agents (software that plans, takes ownership, holds goals in memory), and multimodality (voice, video, image). The model layer is getting more competitive—GPT-4 dropped from $30 to $2 per million tokens in 18 months, with distilled versions at 10 cents. Claude and Gemini gained share; new entrants like SSI, Thinking Machines, and DeepSeek add competition. She advises planning for a multimodel world. At the application layer, code was first: Cursor reached $100M ARR in 12 months with 500K developers and zero salespeople. Code was first because it's structured logical text with deterministic validation, researchers prioritized it for AGI, and engineers built tools for engineers. The 'Cursor for X' playbook means using domain and workflow knowledge as bootstrap, building products that show up informed, collecting and packaging context automatically, orchestrating the right models, and presenting outputs thoughtfully. The prompt is a bug, not a feature. She observes an AI leapfrog effect where conservative, low-tech industries adopt fastest: Sierra resolves 70% of customer service queries, Harvey exceeds $70M ARR, and Open Evidence reaches a third of US doctors weekly. Co-pilots remain underrated—human tolerance for failure reduces as latency increases, so building great augmentation and riding the capability wave is the path of least frustration. On defensibility, she argues execution is the moat: Cursor didn't invent code completion or the model but outexecuted competitors. Jasper, by contrast, had first-mover advantage and raised $125M but was crushed because its product was just prompts and a text box. Hard problems in robotics, biology, material science, and physics require data beyond common crawl and interaction with atoms, not just bits. She concludes we're in the dialup era of AI, the game board keeps getting shaken up with each model release, and engineers—who got the magic first—must be translators for the rest of the world, since 40% of AI economic use is still coding.

sections.title: Introduction and Conviction Fund Background
sections.summary: Sarah Guo introduces herself and Conviction, an AI-native venture fund started ~3 years ago before ChatGPT launch. Previously at Greylock; partner Mike Vernal from Sequoia. Portfolio includes Cursor, Cognition, Mistral, Thinking Machines, Harvey, Open Evidence, Base10. She observes unprecedented user uptake and companies reaching $10-100M run rate faster than any prior tech cycle, and frames the talk around capabilities, market validation, and what to build.

sections.title: AI Capabilities: Reasoning, Agents, and Multimodality
sections.summary: Reasoning is a new vector for scaling intelligence with compute, unlocking high-stakes decisions and systematic search. Agents are defined as software that plans, takes ownership of tasks, holds goals in memory, and tries hypotheses. Agent startups in Embed grant program grew 50% over the past year. Multimodal AI companies (HeyGen, 11 Labs, Midjourney) surpass $50M ARR. Voice expected first in business workflows as a natural communication mode.

sections.title: Model Market Competition and Cost Trends
sections.summary: Model capabilities continue improving across every layer. GPT-4 dropped from $30 to $2 per million tokens in 18 months; distilled versions at 10 cents. Claude cut into OpenAI's market share; Google returned with Gemini. New entrants include SSI, Thinking Machines, and DeepSeek with competitive open-source models. Advice: plan for a multimodel world using tools like OpenRouter and Base10.

sections.title: Application Layer: Code as First Frontier
sections.summary: Code was the first AI killer application. Cursor hit $100M ARR in 12 months with 500K developers and zero salespeople. Cognition is the top committer at many companies. Windsurf being acquired by OpenAI for $3B. Lovable and Bolt each reached $30M ARR in weeks. Code was first because it's structured logical text, much is boilerplate, and it has deterministic validation via tests and compilation—no AGI needed for API endpoints or React components.

sections.title: The Cursor for X Playbook and Workflow Wrappers
sections.summary: Code was first also because researchers prioritized it for AGI and engineers built tools for engineers. The last point is the money point: understanding the workflow intimately made the difference. The playbook for every other industry is 'Cursor for X'—customer-centric, problem-centric builders who understand AI and redesign workflows from first principles. Cursor is not a single model; it orchestrates multiple models for diffs, merges, embeddings, and context packaging with skillful prompting, cursor rules, retrieval that improves with use, and familiar UX. Cursor is a thick wrapper worth $14-15 billion. Generic text boxes are not valuable; domain and workflow knowledge is the bootstrap. Products should show up informed, collect and package context automatically, orchestrate the right models, and present outputs thoughtfully. The prompt is a bug, not a feature—don't make users think.

sections.title: AI Leapfrog Effect in Conservative Industries
sections.summary: Beyond coding, the most conservative low-tech industries seem to be adopting AI fastest—the AI leapfrog effect. Sierra resolves 70% of customer service queries for customers like SiriusXM and ADT. Harvey is well over $70M ARR, essential to legal competitiveness. Open Evidence helps doctors stay current with medical research, reaching a third of US doctors weekly with daily average use. Notable: Sierra's Bret Taylor chairs OpenAI's board; OpenAI was Harvey's seed investor—these insiders aren't fretting about thin wrappers.

sections.title: Co-pilots vs Full Automation and Startup Opportunities
sections.summary: Despite excitement about full automation and agents, co-pilots are still underrated based on revenue data. The Iron Man analogy applies: the suit augments Tony Stark but can also do basic tasks autonomously. Human tolerance for failure reduces dramatically as latency increases, so the path of least frustration is building great augmentation and riding the capability wave. Opportunities span from purpose-fit text generation to previously impossible applications—machines interrogating humans, talking to every customer, root-causing alerts proactively. Hard problems in robotics, biology, material science, and physics require data beyond common crawl and interaction with atoms, not just bits.

sections.title: Defensibility: Execution Is the Moat
sections.summary: Some say stay out of the labs' way, but the uncomfortable truth is execution is the moat in AI. Cursor didn't invent code completion, the model, or its product surface—it outexecuted on every dimension and shipped faster than competitors could copy. Jasper is the counterexample: first-mover advantage, $125M raised, but its product was prompts and a text box—ChatGPT crushed it quickly. Build something thick and stay ahead. Magical AI experiences build customer trust; needed data and context advantages are open for the taking, not reserved for labs.

sections.title: Conclusion: Dialup Era of AI and Engineer's Role
sections.summary: The opportunity is early and massive—we're in the dialup era of AI moving to broadband. Instagram came 4 years after iPhone, Uber 5, DoorDash 6; transformative companies reimagined experiences rather than being first. The game board keeps getting shaken up with each new model release, creating repeated opportunities to win. Engineers got the magic first—40% of AI economic use is still coding, which is not 40% of the world's economic opportunity. Engineers must be translators for the rest of the world and build something revolutionary.
